item.title: ABPlanner: Adaptable Budget Planner for Budget-Constrained Auto-Bidding (KDD 2025)
item.description:
Researchers published ABPlanner, an adaptable budget planner for budget-constrained auto-bidding in online advertising. The framework decomposes the bidding process into shorter, manageable stages, with a high-level budget planner allocating budget across stages and a low-level auto-bidder making bids based on that allocation. The paper was accepted at KDD 2025.

ABPlanner uses a sequential decision-making approach inspired by in-context reinforcement learning. It adjusts budget allocation plans episode by episode, using data from previous episodes as prompts for current decisions. This few-shot adaptation enables the system to quickly adjust to different advertisers without extensive training.

The framework optimizes cumulative value of winning impressions within specified budget constraints — a challenging optimization problem because the value of each impression depends on the competition, user intent, and time of day.

Extensive simulation experiments and real-world A/B testing demonstrated the framework's ability to enhance the cumulative value achieved by auto-bidders. The hierarchical approach — separating budget planning from bid execution — allows each component to specialize and optimize independently.

For practitioners, ABPlanner offers a practical pattern for budget-constrained auto-bidding: use a high-level planner to allocate budget across time periods or campaigns, and a low-level bidder to optimize individual bids within that budget. The in-context learning approach enables quick adaptation to new advertisers without retraining.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05187

item.title: DCMAB: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Real-Time Bidding in Display Advertising (CIKM 2018)
item.description:
Researchers published DCMAB (Distributed Coordinated Multi-Agent Bidding), which formulates bidding optimization with multi-agent reinforcement learning for display advertising. The approach was evaluated on industry-scaled real-world data.

The key insight is clustering advertisers into groups, with each cluster assigned a strategic bidding agent. This scales the approach to large advertiser populations while maintaining meaningful learning. The coordination mechanism among agents balances competition and cooperation — agents learn to bid strategically without driving up prices through excessive competition.

Cluster-based bidding outperforms both single-agent approaches and bandit-based methods. Coordinated bidding achieves better overall objectives compared to purely self-interested bidding agents, demonstrating that cooperation among advertisers (through the platform's coordination mechanism) can improve outcomes for everyone.

For practitioners, DCMAB demonstrates that multi-agent RL can be practically applied to ad bidding by using clustering to scale. The coordination mechanism is important — without it, agents may learn to compete aggressively, driving up costs without improving outcomes.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.09756

item.title: PDCaSA: Proactive Detection of Seasonal Ads with Multimodal LLMs Achieving 0.97 F1 Score
item.description:
Researchers published PDCaSA (Proactive Detection and Calibration of Seasonal Advertisements), leveraging multimodal large language models (MLMs) to detect seasonality in advertisements. The MLM-based approach achieved 0.97 top F1 score on their in-house benchmark.

Seasonal ads — those tied to holidays, events, or seasons — require special handling in ad ranking systems. If a Christmas ad continues to be shown in January, it provides poor user experience and wastes advertiser budget. PDCaSA proactively detects seasonal content so ranking systems can calibrate accordingly.

The paper envisions MLMs serving three roles in the detection system: teacher for knowledge distillation (transferring seasonal knowledge to smaller models), machine labeler (generating annotations for training data), and part of an ensembled and tiered system (contributing to a multi-layer seasonality detection pipeline).

The 0.97 F1 score indicates near-perfect detection accuracy. For practitioners, this work demonstrates that multimodal LLMs can be effectively applied to ad quality tasks beyond ranking — detecting seasonal relevance is a practical problem that affects both user experience and advertiser ROI.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00780

item.title: CTRL: Connecting Collaborative and Language Models for CTR Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published CTRL, a framework that bridges collaborative filtering models with pre-trained language models (PLMs) for CTR prediction. The approach is described as industrial-friendly and model-agnostic with superior inference efficiency, outperforming state-of-the-art CTR models on three public datasets plus a large-scale industrial recommender system.

Traditional CTR models use one-hot encoding on tabular data, discarding essential semantic information. Prior PLM-based approaches are computationally expensive and suffer from low efficiency, neglecting collaborative relations. CTRL addresses both limitations by treating tabular and textual data as two separate modalities.

The architecture processes tabular data through a collaborative CTR model and textual data through a pre-trained language model, then performs cross-modal knowledge alignment to fine-grained align and integrate collaborative and semantic signals. Crucially, the lightweight collaborative model can be deployed online for efficient serving after being fine-tuned with supervised signals — the heavy PLM is not needed at inference time.

For practitioners, CTRL demonstrates a practical pattern for incorporating language model knowledge into CTR prediction: use PLMs during training to enrich semantic understanding, then distill that knowledge into lightweight collaborative models for production serving.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02841

item.title: LLaCTR: Lightweight LLM-Enhanced CTR via Field-Level Semantic Knowledge Distillation
item.description:
Researchers published LLaCTR, a lightweight LLM-enhanced CTR method that employs a field-level enhancement paradigm. The method was integrated with six representative CTR models and evaluated across four datasets, showing superior performance in terms of both effectiveness and efficiency over existing LLM-enhanced methods.

LLaCTR first utilizes LLMs to distill crucial and lightweight semantic knowledge from small-scale feature fields through self-supervised field-feature fine-tuning. It then leverages this field-level semantic knowledge to enhance both feature representation and feature interactions.

The key insight is operating at the field level rather than the instance or entity level, which reduces computational overhead compared to prior LLM-enhanced CTR approaches that require extensive processing of detailed textual descriptions for large-scale instances or user/item entities.

For practitioners, LLaCTR offers a more efficient way to incorporate LLM knowledge into CTR models. By distilling at the field level rather than the instance level, the approach scales better to large datasets while still capturing semantic understanding that traditional embedding-based approaches miss.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14057

item.title: FCN: Fusing Exponential and Linear Cross Networks for CTR Prediction (KDD 2026)
item.description:
Researchers published FCN (Fusing Exponential and Linear Cross Network) for CTR prediction, achieving new state-of-the-art performance across six datasets. The paper was accepted at KDD 2026.

FCN consists of two core sub-networks: a Linear Cross Network (LCN) that captures feature interactions with linear growth, and an Exponential Cross Network (ECN) that captures feature interactions with exponential growth. Both operate explicitly rather than relying on implicit DNN learning.

Key components include a Self-Mask Operation that filters noise layer by layer and reduces cross network parameters by half, and a Tri-BCE Loss that provides tailored supervision signals for each network.

The paper identifies four limitations of prior DCN-family models: explicit interaction methods underperform vs. implicit DNN, high-order interactions contain overlooked noise, different interaction branches lack appropriate supervision signals, and high-order interactions are implicit and non-interpretable. FCN addresses all four.

For practitioners, FCN demonstrates that explicit feature interaction modeling can match or exceed implicit DNN approaches when properly designed. The linear and exponential cross networks capture different interaction patterns, and the self-mask mechanism efficiently filters noise from high-order interactions.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13349

item.title: FinalMLP: Enhanced Two-Stream MLP Model for CTR Prediction (AAAI 2023)
item.description:
Researchers published FinalMLP, an enhanced two-stream MLP model for CTR prediction that achieves better performance than many sophisticated two-stream CTR models. The paper was accepted at AAAI 2023.

The key insight is that a well-tuned two-stream MLP model that simply combines two MLPs can achieve surprisingly good performance. FinalMLP enhances this with two innovations: a Feature Gating Layer that enables differentiated feature inputs (each stream receives tailored feature representations), and an Interaction Aggregation Layer that effectively fuses stream-level interactions across the two streams.

The paper notes that MLP serves as a core component in many deep CTR prediction models but is inefficient in learning multiplicative feature interactions. Existing two-stream models like DeepFM and DCN pair an MLP with a specialized interaction network. FinalMLP's insight is that the MLP stream learns interactions implicitly, and enhancing this with gating and aggregation mechanisms yields strong results without explicit interaction modeling.

Evaluated on four open benchmark datasets plus an online A/B test in an industrial system, FinalMLP demonstrates that simple architectures with proper design can match or exceed more complex approaches.

For practitioners, FinalMLP offers a simpler alternative to complex CTR architectures. The two-stream MLP with feature gating and interaction aggregation is easy to implement and tune, yet competitive with more sophisticated models.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.00902

item.title: GDCN: Gated Deep Cross Network with Field-Level Dimension Optimization for CTR (CIKM 2023)
item.description:
Researchers published GDCN (Gated Deep Cross Network) for CTR prediction, addressing three challenges: high-order decay, interpretability, and redundancy. The paper was accepted at CIKM 2023.

GDCN introduces an information gate in each order of the cross network that dynamically filters which feature interactions are important. This addresses the high-order decay problem where performance drops as interaction order increases — not all high-order interactions are useful, and the gate learns to suppress noisy ones.

A Field-level Dimension Optimization (FDO) component learns condensed dimensions for each feature field based on their importance, reducing redundant parameters particularly in the embedding layer. This addresses the parameter bloat problem in large-scale CTR models.

Experiments on five datasets demonstrate effectiveness, superiority, and interpretability. The gating mechanism provides interpretability by revealing which feature interactions the model considers important for each prediction.

For practitioners, GDCN offers a principled approach to scaling cross networks. The gating mechanism prevents high-order interactions from degrading performance, and the field-level dimension optimization reduces model size without sacrificing accuracy.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04635

item.title: MEDA: Multi-Epoch Learning with Data Augmentation Solving One-Epoch Overfitting in CTR Models
item.description:
Researchers published MEDA (Multi-Epoch learning with Data Augmentation), addressing the one-epoch overfitting problem in CTR models where performance notably declines at the start of the second epoch. The root cause is overfitting of the embedding layer due to high-dimensional data sparsity.

MEDA supports both non-continual and continual learning scenarios and can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep CTR models. The framework reduces the dependency of the embedding layer on subsequent training data or the MLP layers through data augmentation that trains the MLP with varied embedding spaces.

A key finding is that pre-trained MLP layers can adapt to new embedding spaces, suggesting MLP layers learn a matching function focused on the relative relationships among embeddings rather than their absolute positions. This insight enables multi-epoch training by varying the embedding space across epochs.

The paper describes MEDA as the first multi-epoch training strategy tailored for deep CTR prediction models. It showed significant benefits in a real-world online advertising system and can also address the forgetting or overfitting dilemma in retraining and catastrophic forgetting problems.

For practitioners, MEDA solves a common practical problem: CTR models are typically trained for only one epoch because additional epochs degrade performance. This wastes data and limits model quality. MEDA enables multi-epoch training, potentially improving model quality without the overfitting penalty.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01607

item.title: DPN: Deep Pattern Network with Target Pattern Attention for CTR Prediction (SIGIR 2024)
item.description:
Researchers published DPN (Deep Pattern Network) for CTR prediction, accepted at SIGIR 2024. The model introduces Target Pattern Attention (TPA), an extension of Target Attention that models pattern-level dependencies in user behavior data.

DPN addresses three challenges in behavior pattern modeling: inclusion of unrelated items within behavior patterns, data sparsity in behavior patterns, and computational complexity arising from numerous patterns. The model uses a target-aware attention mechanism to efficiently retrieve target-related user behavior patterns.

A self-supervised learning pre-training paradigm refines user behavior patterns while promoting dependency learning within sparse patterns. This helps the model learn meaningful patterns even when behavioral data is limited.

DPN focuses on modeling user behavior patterns rather than just co-occurrence relationships between the target item and items previously interacted with. User interactions contain diverse behavior patterns indicative of a spectrum of habitual paradigms.

For practitioners, DPN demonstrates that pattern-level attention can capture richer user intent than item-level attention. By recognizing that users follow behavioral patterns (not just individual item interactions), the model can make better predictions about future engagement.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11456

item.title: FeSAIL: Feature Staleness Aware Incremental Learning for CTR Prediction (IJCAI 2023)
item.description:
Researchers published FeSAIL (Feature Staleness Aware Incremental Learning) for CTR prediction, addressing the problem of feature staleness in incremental model training. The paper extends work published at IJCAI 2023.

When feature embeddings don't appear in the current incremental data batch, they become stale, causing performance degradation on samples containing stale features. FeSAIL addresses this with two components:

  • Staleness Aware Sampling (SAS): Samples a fixed number of stale samples with high sampling efficiency, enabling adaptive replay of underrepresented features during incremental training.
  • Staleness Aware Regularization (SAR): Provides fine-grained control of feature embedding updating, preventing stale embeddings from drifting too far or being updated too aggressively.

FeSAIL is model-agnostic — it can be instantiated with any general deep learning-based CTR prediction model. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show it outperforms various state-of-the-art methods.

For practitioners, FeSAIL addresses a practical challenge in continuous model training: as new data arrives, some features may not appear in the current batch, causing their embeddings to become stale. This is particularly problematic for long-tail features that appear infrequently.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02844

item.title: NCS4CVR: Neuron-Connection Sharing for Multi-Task CVR Prediction in Video Recommendations
item.description:
Researchers published NCS4CVR, proposing neuron-connection level sharing for multi-task CVR prediction. This represents the first time a fine-grained CTR&CVR sharing method at the neuron connection level has been proposed. The system was successfully deployed in an industry video recommender system serving major traffic.

The CVR data sparsity problem — CVR involves much fewer samples than CTR — is a fundamental challenge. Existing multi-task approaches use coarse-grained sub-network/layer sharing, which introduces task conflicts because different tasks may need different representations at the same layer.

NCS4CVR can automatically and flexibly learn which neuron weights are shared or not shared without artificial experience. The motivation is that users exhibit different fine-grained content feature preferences between deep consumption (conversion) and click behavior.

The approach outperforms both single-task and layer-level sharing models in offline and online experiments. By learning sharing at the neuron level rather than the layer level, the model can share useful representations while keeping task-specific ones separate.

For practitioners, NCS4CVR demonstrates that the granularity of parameter sharing in multi-task learning matters. Layer-level sharing is too coarse — neuron-level sharing allows more flexible knowledge transfer between CTR and CVR tasks while avoiding negative transfer.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.09872

item.title: MLoRA: Multi-Domain Low-Rank Adaptive Network for CTR Prediction at Alibaba (RecSys 2024)
item.description:
Alibaba deployed MLoRA (Multi-Domain Low-Rank Adaptive Network) for multi-domain CTR prediction, accepted at RecSys 2024. Online A/B testing confirmed superiority and flexibility in production.

MLoRA introduces a specialized LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) module for each domain, addressing data sparsity and disparate data distributions across domains. Existing methods introduce specific-domain modules for each domain, significantly increasing model parameters and leading to insufficient training. MLoRA uses low-rank adaptation to mitigate this.

The approach is model-agnostic — it can be applied to various deep-learning models as a plug-in module. Each domain gets its own LoRA module rather than full domain-specific parameters, making it parameter-efficient.

For practitioners, MLoRA demonstrates that LoRA — originally developed for efficiently fine-tuning LLMs — can be applied to multi-domain CTR prediction. The low-rank adaptation approach enables domain-specific modeling without the parameter explosion of full domain-specific modules.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08913

item.title: OptFusion: Automated Fusion Learning for Deep CTR Prediction Models (WSDM 2025)
item.description:
Researchers published OptFusion, which automates fusion learning in deep CTR prediction models, covering both connection learning and operation selection. The paper was accepted at WSDM 2025.

While feature interaction components have received significant research attention in CTR models, fusion design has been relatively neglected. Two common fusion approaches — stacked and parallel — suffer from pre-determined fusion connections and fixed fusion operations. Changes in fusion design lead to varying performance, underscoring fusion's critical role.

OptFusion uses a one-shot learning algorithm that tackles connection learning and operation selection concurrently. This automates the design process that was previously manual or constrained to specific settings.

For practitioners, OptFusion demonstrates that how model components are combined matters as much as which components are used. The automated fusion learning approach can discover better architectures than manual design, potentially improving CTR model performance without changing the underlying feature interaction modules.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15731

item.title: Unified Low-Rank Compression for CTR Prediction: 3-5X Model Size Reduction with Higher AUC (KDD 2024)
item.description:
Researchers published a unified low-rank compression framework for CTR prediction that achieves 3-5X model size reduction while the compressed models achieve both faster inference and higher AUC than the uncompressed original models. The paper was accepted at KDD 2024.

The framework addresses three challenges: reducing model sizes for edge devices, accelerating inference, and preserving original model capabilities post-compression. Unlike prior approaches that compress model weights directly, this framework locally compresses output features.

A key finding is that even with the most classic matrix decomposition SVD method, the framework can achieve better performance than the original model. This is counterintuitive — compression typically sacrifices accuracy, but this approach actually improves it.

The framework is applicable to both embedding tables and MLP layers across various CTR models, making it a general-purpose compression tool.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that model compression can be a win-win: smaller models that are both faster and more accurate. The output feature compression approach is novel and effective, offering a practical path to deploying CTR models in resource-constrained environments.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18146

item.title: GateNet: Gating-Enhanced Deep Network for CTR Prediction with Feature Embedding and Hidden Gates
item.description:
Researchers published GateNet, which introduces gating mechanisms into standard deep CTR models. Two types of gates are proposed: Feature Embedding Gates (applied to the embedding layer to select salient latent information) and Hidden Gates (applied to MLP layers to implicitly capture high-order interactions more effectively).

The gating modules are evaluated on top of FM, DeepFM, and xDeepFM, boosting performance on all datasets. The design is modular — the gates can be plugged into existing DNN-based CTR architectures without major changes.

The motivation comes from the success of gating mechanisms in CV and NLP (LSTM, GRU, attention). The paper cites research showing that gating mechanisms improve the trainability of non-convex deep neural networks.

For practitioners, GateNet offers a simple, plug-and-play enhancement for existing CTR models. The Feature Embedding Gate helps the model focus on the most relevant features, while the Hidden Gate helps capture important feature interactions in the MLP layers.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.03519

item.title: Fi-GNN: Feature Interaction via Graph Neural Networks for CTR Prediction (CIKM 2019)
item.description:
Researchers published Fi-GNN (Feature Interaction Graph Neural Networks) for CTR prediction, representing multi-field features as a graph structure where nodes correspond to feature fields and edges represent interactions between fields. The paper was accepted at CIKM 2019.

The core insight is that the simple unstructured combination of feature fields in existing CTR models limits the capability to model sophisticated interactions. By leveraging graph representations, Fi-GNN captures complex feature interactions in a flexible and explicit fashion while providing good model explanations.

Feature interaction modeling is reframed as node interaction modeling on the graph, allowing the model to learn which feature fields interact with each other and how. This is more expressive than fixed interaction patterns used in DCN or DeepFM.

For practitioners, Fi-GNN demonstrates that graph-based approaches can capture feature interactions that fixed-architecture models miss. The graph structure also provides interpretability — by examining the learned edges, practitioners can understand which feature interactions the model considers important.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.05552

item.title: Calibration-then-Calculation: Variance Reduced Metric Framework for Deep CTR Models
item.description:
Researchers published the Calibration-then-Calculation framework, addressing the variance problem in neural network evaluation metrics for CTR prediction. The variance stems from the inherent randomness in the training process, and running training multiple times to mitigate this is computationally prohibitive.

The framework proposes a two-phase approach: first calibrate the loss metric, then calculate the evaluation metric. This reduces variance in conventional metrics, enhancing the accuracy in detecting effective modeling improvements when comparing model iterations.

This is a practical problem that every CTR team faces: when you make a model change, how do you know if the improvement is real or just noise? High variance in evaluation metrics makes it difficult to detect genuine improvements, leading to either wasted compute on false positives or missed opportunities from false negatives.

For practitioners, this framework offers a principled approach to model evaluation that reduces the number of experiments needed to detect genuine improvements. This can significantly accelerate the model development cycle by reducing false positives and false negatives in A/B test decisions.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16692

item.title: EOCA: Expected Transaction Value Optimization for Precise Marketing at Tencent FinTech
item.description:
Researchers published EOCA (ETV Optimized Customer Allocation) for maximizing the total expected transaction value (ETV) of recommended funds on Tencent's LiCaiTong wealth management platform. The paper was accepted at the DLP@RecSys Workshop.

Traditional recommendation systems optimize CTR or CVR, but mutual fund purchases have highly variable transaction amounts even for the same product. The platform must estimate customers' purchase amount for each delivered fund and allocate impressions to optimize total ETV.

EOCA operates within a Guaranteed Delivery (GD) strategy where fund companies require minimum impressions. This is the first attempt to solve the GD problem for financial product promotions based on customer purchase amount prediction.

For practitioners, EOCA demonstrates that optimizing for transaction value rather than just click or conversion rates can significantly improve outcomes in financial advertising. The approach is applicable to any advertising scenario where conversion values vary widely (luxury goods, real estate, financial products).

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01525

item.title: Learning to Create Better Ads: Collaborative Ad Creative Refinement from A/B Test Data (CIKM 2020)
item.description:
Researchers published a method for learning to create better ads through collaborative learning across multiple advertisers' A/B test data. The paper was accepted at CIKM 2020.

The system addresses three tasks: ad text generation (given an inferior creative, generate improved text), keyphrase recommendation (suggest keyphrases for new ad text), and image tag recommendation (recommend image tags to select new images).

The ad text generation model uses an encoder-decoder architecture with a copy mechanism that allows some words from the inferior input text to be copied to the output while simultaneously incorporating new words associated with higher CTR. The keyphrase and image tag recommendation use a deep relevance matching model.

Training uses pairwise examples formed from A/B tests across multiple advertisers — pairs of inferior and superior ad creatives. This collaborative approach leverages data from many advertisers to learn what makes ads effective, rather than relying on each advertiser's limited data alone.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that A/B test data from ad creative experiments can be used to train models that automatically improve ad creatives. The collaborative approach — learning across advertisers — is particularly valuable for small advertisers with limited experimentation data.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.07467

item.title: Predicting Online Video Ad Effects with Multimodal Deep Learning: 0.695 Correlation Coefficient
item.description:
Researchers published a method for predicting the CTR of video advertisements using multimodal deep learning. The approach achieved a correlation coefficient of 0.695, up from a baseline of 0.487. The paper was presented at ICPR 2020.

The multimodal approach leverages three modalities: video features, text features, and metadata features. Metadata is split into categorical and continuous types, each properly separated and normalized. Additional regularization layers are inserted to combat overfitting given limited training data.

The improvement from 0.487 to 0.695 correlation coefficient is substantial — it means the model can predict video ad effectiveness with reasonable accuracy before the ad is shown. This enables advertisers to optimize their video creatives before spending budget on underperforming ads.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that multimodal approaches — combining video, text, and metadata — can significantly improve video ad effectiveness prediction. The proper handling of different metadata types and the regularization for data-scarce settings are practical techniques for video ad optimization.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.11851

item.title: Hierarchical LoRA MoE for Efficient CTR Model Scaling at Meta
item.description:
Researchers published Hierarchical LoRA MoE for efficient CTR model scaling, combining Low-Rank Adaptation with Mixture-of-Experts architecture. This approach enables scaling CTR models without the prohibitive parameter growth of traditional scaling approaches.

The hierarchical structure allows the model to share common knowledge across domains while maintaining domain-specific expertise through LoRA modules. The MoE architecture routes different inputs to different experts, enabling specialization without interference.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that LoRA and MoE — techniques popular in LLM research — can be effectively combined for CTR model scaling. The hierarchical structure enables efficient parameter sharing across multiple prediction tasks and domains.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10432

item.title: DeI2N: Deep Evolutional Instant Interest Network for Trigger-Induced Recommendation (WSDM 2024)
item.description:
Researchers published DEI2N (Deep Evolutional Instant Interest Network) for CTR prediction in trigger-induced recommendation (TIR), where users explicitly express instant interests via trigger items. The paper was accepted at WSDM 2024.

TIR is common on platforms like Alibaba and Amazon where users trigger recommendations by interacting with specific items. DEI2N addresses three limitations of previous methods: neglecting temporal information of user behaviors, not modeling dynamic changes in instant interest during scrolling, and ignoring interactions between trigger and target items.

The model includes three key components: a User Instant Interest Modeling Layer that predicts dynamic changes in instant interest intensity as the user scrolls, temporal information integration for time-aware user behavior modeling, and an interaction layer that learns better interactions between trigger and target items.

Online A/B testing confirms superiority over existing baselines in real-world production environments. For practitioners, DEI2N demonstrates that trigger-induced recommendation requires specialized modeling — the user's explicit trigger provides strong signal about instant interest that should be explicitly modeled.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.07769

item.title: Personalized Ad Recommendation: Ranker-Based Policy for Click Sparsity in Contextual Bandits
item.description:
Researchers published a ranker-based policy for personalized advertisement recommendation that significantly alleviates the problem of click sparsity. The approach uses AUC ranking loss instead of classification loss for training contextual bandit policies.

In personalized ad recommendation, the system displays one of K ads to a user based on their profile/context. A core challenge is extreme click sparsity — very few users actually click on ads. Traditional classifier-based policies struggle because the positive class (clicks) is extremely rare.

The ranker-based policy, trained with AUC ranking loss, yields improvement in CTR compared to classifier-based contextual bandit policies, especially under conditions of extreme click sparsity. By framing the problem as ranking rather than classification, the approach focuses on relative ordering rather than absolute probability estimation.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that the choice of loss function matters significantly for ad recommendation under sparse feedback. AUC-based ranking losses can outperform standard classification losses when positive examples are rare — a common situation in advertising.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.01870

item.title: Uplift Modeling with Continuous Treatments: Predict-Then-Optimize Approach for Ad Targeting
item.description:
Researchers published a predict-then-optimize framework for uplift modeling with continuous treatments, extending traditional binary treatment uplift modeling to continuous-valued treatments. The framework uses Integer Linear Programming for dose allocation under budget constraints.

Traditional uplift modeling uses binary treatments (show ad vs. don't show ad), but many advertising scenarios involve continuous treatments — different ad frequencies, bid amounts, or discount levels. The framework estimates Conditional Average Dose Responses (CADRs) and optimizes treatment allocation using ILP.

The approach supports fairness constraints and adapted objective functions accounting for instance-dependent costs and benefits. This is important for advertising platforms that need to balance advertiser ROI with user experience.

For practitioners, this work extends uplift modeling beyond simple binary treatment decisions to continuous optimization problems common in advertising — how much to bid, how frequently to show ads, what discount to offer.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09232

item.title: RecSys with Distribution-Free Reliability Guarantees: FDR Control for Recommendation Diversity
item.description:
Researchers published a method for adding distribution-free reliability guarantees to recommendation systems. The approach provides rigorous finite-sample control of the false discovery rate (FDR), regardless of the unknown data distribution.

The method builds on a pre-trained ranking model and adds a post-hoc calibration layer that provides reliability guarantees on the recommendation set output. Pairwise comparisons from the ranking model are distilled into user-facing output, enabling principled integration of multiple objectives.

Specifically, the approach enables optimizing for recommendation diversity subject to a user-specified level of FDR control. This is valuable for ad systems that need to balance relevance with diversity — showing only the highest-predicted-CTR ads may create filter bubbles.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that statistical guarantees can be added to recommendation systems post-hoc, without retraining the underlying model. The FDR control ensures that the system doesn't over-recommend irrelevant items while maintaining diversity.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01609

item.title: MA-DNN: Memory Augmented DNN for CTR Prediction with External Memory Vectors (DLP-KDD 2019)
item.description:
Researchers published MA-DNN (Memory Augmented DNN) for CTR prediction, using two external memory vectors for each user that memorize high-level abstractions of what a user possibly likes and dislikes. The paper was accepted at DLP-KDD 2019.

MA-DNN is positioned as a compromise between stateless models (DNN, which considers each target ad independently) and stateful models (RNN, which models temporal dependency between sequential behaviors). MA-DNN has memory of historical likes/dislikes while being as simple as a DNN.

The memory component is modular — it can be augmented to other models as well (e.g., the Wide&Deep model). This makes it a flexible enhancement for existing CTR architectures.

For practitioners, MA-DNN offers a simpler alternative to RNN-based sequential models for capturing user history. The external memory vectors provide a compact representation of user preferences without the complexity of recurrent architectures.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.04667

item.title: Leaf-FM: Learnable Feature Generation Factorization Machine for CTR Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published Leaf-FM, which automatically generates features from original feature embeddings by learning transformation functions. The model achieves comparable performance with deep learning models like DNN and AutoInt on Avazu and Malware datasets while maintaining the same online serving complexity as standard FM.

Traditional feature engineering for CTR prediction relies on manual expertise — transforming continuous features to power forms or creating cross features. Leaf-FM automates this by learning transformation functions that generate new features from existing embeddings.

Three concrete variants are proposed based on different strategies for combining original and generated features. The key advantage is that Leaf-FM has the same serving complexity as FM, making it practical for production deployment while achieving accuracy comparable to much more complex models.

For practitioners, Leaf-FM demonstrates that automated feature generation can match the performance of deep learning models while maintaining the simplicity and speed of factorization machines.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12024

item.title: TF4CTR: Twin Focus Framework for Adaptive Sample Differentiation in CTR Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published TF4CTR (Twin Focus Framework) for CTR prediction, identifying two core limitations in existing models: undifferentiated samples (models learn easy samples while ignoring hard ones) and inconsistent supervision (different encoders receive the same supervision signals).

The framework includes three plug-and-play components: SSEM (Sample Selection Embedding Module) that differentiates samples and assigns appropriate encoders, TF Loss that provides tailored supervision signals to both simple and complex encoders, and DFM (Dynamic Fusion Module) that dynamically fuses feature interaction information.

The framework is model-agnostic — it can enhance various existing CTR baselines. Experiments on five real-world datasets confirm effectiveness and compatibility.

For practitioners, TF4CTR addresses the common problem of hard sample mining in CTR prediction. By differentiating between easy and hard samples and providing tailored supervision, the model can focus its capacity on the samples that matter most.

Sources:

item.title: EGIN: Lightweight Graph Interest Network for CTR Prediction in E-Commerce Search
item.description:
Researchers published EGIN (End-to-end Graph Interest Network) for CTR prediction in e-commerce search. The model captures correlation and sequential information of query and item efficiently through a heterogeneous graph, with relatively low training cost compared to the main CTR prediction task.

Unlike prior graph-based methods that rely on item sequential information from user behaviors, EGIN incorporates query's sequential signal and query-item correlation via a heterogeneous graph built from the search system. This captures search-specific signals that recommendation-focused graph models miss.

The end-to-end training approach means graph embedding learning shares the same training input and is jointly trained with CTR prediction, simplifying deployment at scale.

For practitioners, EGIN demonstrates that search-specific graph features — query-item correlations and query-level sequential patterns — can improve CTR prediction in e-commerce search. The lightweight design ensures the graph component doesn't add significant serving latency.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17745

item.title: Mutual Learning for Finetuning CTR Prediction Models: Up to 0.66% Relative Improvement
item.description:
Researchers published a mutual learning approach for finetuning CTR prediction models, achieving up to 0.66% relative improvement. Unlike standard knowledge distillation that assumes a large teacher and small student, mutual learning operates between models of similar complexity.

The motivation is that CTR models are relatively simple architecturally — the performance gap between complex and simple models is not very large. Standard distillation's cumbersome vs. tiny distinction is ill-suited for this setting.

Mutual learning allows all models to improve each other during training, rather than one-way knowledge transfer. This is evaluated on Criteo and Avazu datasets.

For practitioners, mutual learning offers a simple technique for improving CTR models without architectural changes. Train two similar models together and let them teach each other — a low-cost enhancement that can provide measurable improvements.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12087

item.title: Regularized Adversarial Sampling and Deep Time-Aware Attention for CTR Prediction (CIKM 2019)
item.description:
Researchers published a time-aware attention model with regularized adversarial sampling for CTR prediction. The paper was accepted at CIKM 2019.

The paper addresses a gap where existing CTR models neglect the importance of temporal signals when embedding users' historical clicking records. Two temporal signal types are used: absolute temporal signals for expressing periodic behaviors, and relative temporal signals for expressing temporal relations between items.

A regularized adversarial sampling strategy targets negative sampling to ease the classification imbalance of CTR data. It makes use of the strong guidance provided by observed negative CTR samples, significantly improves training efficiency, and can be co-trained with the time-aware attention model seamlessly.

For practitioners, this work highlights the importance of temporal features in CTR prediction. When users clicked matters as much as what they clicked — time-of-day, day-of-week, and recency all carry important signal about user intent.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00886

item.title: CETN: Contrast-Enhanced Through Network for CTR Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published CETN (Contrast-enhanced Through Network) for CTR prediction, combining contrastive learning with feature interaction modeling. The approach enhances CTR prediction by learning better feature representations through contrastive objectives.

Contrastive learning has been successful in CV and NLP for learning robust representations. CETN applies this to CTR prediction, using contrastive objectives to improve the quality of feature embeddings before they enter the feature interaction layers.

For practitioners, CETN demonstrates that contrastive learning can improve CTR model performance by learning better feature representations. The technique can be combined with existing CTR architectures as a pre-training or co-training objective.

Sources:

item.title: FINN: Feature Interaction Neural Network with 3D Relation Tensor for CTR Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published FINN (Feature Interaction based Neural Network) for CTR prediction, modeling feature interaction via a 3-dimensional relation tensor. The approach outperforms state-of-the-art deep models like PNN and DeepFM.

FINN addresses the limitation of existing approaches that calculate feature interactions using simple inner products or element-wise products. The 3D tensor provides representations for feature interactions on the bottom layer with non-linearity of neural network in modeling higher-order feature interactions.

The finding that feature interaction contains significant information for better CTR prediction validates the importance of explicit interaction modeling in CTR architectures.

For practitioners, FINN demonstrates that richer feature interaction representations can improve CTR prediction. The 3D tensor approach captures more complex interaction patterns than simple vector products.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05312

item.title: Is Attention All You Need for CTR Prediction? General Framework via Self-Attention (SIGIR 2021)
item.description:
Researchers published a general neural network framework built on self-attention for CTR prediction, using the discrete choice model in economics to redefine the problem. The paper was accepted at SIGIR 2021.

The authors argue that most existing CTR prediction models align with their proposed general framework. They examine the expressive power and model complexity and discuss potential extensions to existing models.

This work provides a unifying theoretical perspective on CTR prediction architectures, showing that diverse models (DeepFM, DCN, DIN, etc.) can be understood as special cases of a general attention-based framework. This theoretical grounding helps practitioners understand when and why different architectures work.

For practitioners, this framework provides a principled way to design and evaluate CTR architectures by understanding their relationship to the general attention-based formulation.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05563

item.title: CTR Prediction Using Graph Neural Networks and Online Learning: 1.7% AUC Improvement
item.description:
Researchers published a study combining Graph Neural Networks with Online Learning for CTR prediction, achieving 0.7585 test AUC compared to 0.7417 for offline models — a 1.7 percentage point improvement. The approach combines collaborative filtering signals from user-item interaction graphs with online learning for dynamic adaptation.

The GNN captures collaborative signals from user-item interaction graphs — users who interact with similar items may have similar preferences. The online learning component adapts to dynamic user behavior, updating the model as new interactions arrive.

The application domains span online advertising, e-commerce, query suggestions in search engines, and friend recommendation in social networks.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that combining graph-based collaborative filtering with online learning can improve CTR prediction. The graph captures structural relationships in user-item interactions, while online learning keeps the model fresh as user behavior evolves.

Sources:

item.title: Impression Allocation and Policy Search in Display Advertising via Multi-Agent RL
item.description:
Researchers published a method for impression allocation between guaranteed contracts and real-time bidding in display advertising. The approach uses auction-based formulation where each guaranteed contract submits virtual bids for individual impressions, with multi-agent reinforcement learning to adjust bids from each contract.

The key challenges are ensuring incentive compatibility in RTB and handling unstable traffic patterns (impression volume and bid landscape changing). The MARL approach is described as simple, converging efficiently, and scalable.

For practitioners, this work addresses the fundamental problem of how publishers should allocate impressions between direct-sold guaranteed campaigns and programmatic RTB. The auction-based approach with MARL provides a principled solution that adapts to changing market conditions.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07073

item.title: Field-Embedded Factorization Machines for CTR Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published Field-Embedded Factorization Machines for CTR prediction, enhancing standard factorization machines with field-aware embeddings. The approach captures field-level interactions more effectively than standard FM.

Factorization Machines are a foundational model for CTR prediction, but they treat all features equally without considering which field each feature belongs to. Field-embedded FM addresses this by learning field-specific embedding spaces that capture the different semantic meanings of features from different fields.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that field awareness — knowing which field a feature belongs to — can improve FM-based CTR prediction. This is a simple enhancement that can be applied to existing FM models.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.09931

item.title: Pairwise Ranking Loss for Multi-Task Learning in Ad Recommender Systems
item.description:
Researchers published PWiseR (Pairwise Ranking Loss) for multi-task learning in ad recommender systems. The key insight is that a conversion (y_cvr=1) necessitates a preceding click (y_ctr=1), and this constraint should be reflected in the loss function.

Traditional multi-task learning treats CTR and CVR prediction as independent tasks, ignoring the logical dependency between them. PWiseR uses pairwise ranking loss that respects this dependency — the model learns that CVR predictions should be lower than CTR predictions for the same impression.

For practitioners, PWiseR demonstrates that incorporating task dependencies into multi-task learning can improve both CTR and CVR prediction. The pairwise ranking loss is a simple modification that respects the logical structure of the advertising funnel.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02163

item.title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Meta-Reinforcement Learning for Cross-Channel Bidding
item.description:
Researchers published a hierarchical multi-agent meta-reinforcement learning approach for cross-channel bidding in online advertising. The method enables rapid adaptation to new advertising channels by leveraging meta-learning across existing channels.

Cross-channel bidding is challenging because each advertising channel (search, display, social, video) has different auction dynamics, user behaviors, and competitive landscapes. Traditional RL approaches require extensive training for each new channel. Meta-learning enables the system to quickly adapt to new channels by transferring knowledge from existing ones.

For practitioners, this approach addresses the practical challenge of expanding advertising to new channels. Instead of training a new bidding agent from scratch for each channel, meta-learning enables rapid adaptation with minimal data.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19064

item.title: Compress Cross and Scale: Multi-Level Compression Cross Networks (MLCC) for Efficient CTR
item.description:
Researchers published MLCC (Multi-Level Compression Cross Networks) for CTR and conversion rate prediction, achieving up to 0.52 AUC improvement while reducing model parameters and FLOPs by up to 26X.

MLCC addresses the scaling problem in cross networks — as models grow larger, the computational cost increases without proportional accuracy gains. By compressing at multiple levels (embedding, cross layer, and network levels), MLCC achieves better accuracy with fewer parameters.

For practitioners, MLCC demonstrates that compression and accuracy are not necessarily at odds. Multi-level compression can actually improve model quality by removing redundant parameters while maintaining the important interactions.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12041

item.title: Deep Situation-Aware Interaction Network for CTR Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published the Deep Situation-Aware Interaction Network for CTR prediction, which models the situation context in which interactions occur. The approach captures how the same user-item pair may have different interaction outcomes depending on the situational context (time, device, location, etc.).

Traditional CTR models treat interactions as context-independent, but user behavior is heavily influenced by context. A user browsing on mobile during commute has different intent than the same user browsing on desktop at home. Situation-aware modeling captures these nuances.

For practitioners, this work highlights the importance of situational context in CTR prediction. The same user may have very different CTR for the same ad depending on when, where, and how they encounter it.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12298

item.title: An Analysis of Entire Space Multi-Task Models for Post-Click Conversion Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published an empirical analysis of entire space multi-task models for post-click conversion prediction in mobile app advertising. The key finding is that several different approaches result in similar levels of positive transfer, suggesting that the multi-task learning paradigm itself matters more than the specific architecture.

The study evaluates multiple multi-task learning approaches for CVR prediction, including ESMM (Entire Space Multi-Task Model) and its variants. The finding that different approaches yield similar results is valuable because it suggests practitioners should focus on getting the multi-task formulation right rather than searching for the perfect architecture.

For practitioners, this analysis provides guidance on multi-task CVR modeling: the entire-space formulation (training on all impressions, not just clicks) is more important than the specific multi-task architecture used.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.13475

item.title: Click-Aware Structure Transfer with Sample Weight Assignment for Post-Click CVR Estimation
item.description:
Researchers published CSTWA (Click-Aware Structure Transfer with Sample Weight Assignment) for post-click CVR estimation. The approach addresses the "curse of knowledge problem" when transferring CTR knowledge to CVR tasks.

The curse of knowledge occurs when CTR models learn patterns that are informative for click prediction but misleading for conversion prediction. CSTWA transfers knowledge selectively, using click-aware sample weighting to ensure that only relevant CTR knowledge is transferred to the CVR model.

For practitioners, this work addresses a practical challenge in multi-task ad prediction: how to transfer knowledge between related tasks without negative transfer. The click-aware weighting approach ensures that CTR knowledge helps rather than hurts CVR prediction.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01169

item.title: DADNN: Multi-Scene CTR Prediction via Domain-Aware Deep Neural Network
item.description:
Researchers published DADNN (Domain-Aware Deep Neural Network) for multi-scene CTR prediction. The approach handles multiple advertising scenes (search, display, feed) within a single model by learning scene-specific and scene-shared representations.

Multi-scene prediction is challenging because different advertising scenes have different user behaviors, ad formats, and competitive dynamics. DADNN addresses this by learning domain-aware representations that capture both the commonalities and differences across scenes.

For practitioners, DADNN demonstrates that multi-scene CTR prediction can be more effective than training separate models for each scene. The domain-aware approach enables knowledge sharing across scenes while maintaining scene-specific specialization.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.11938

item.title: Hierarchical Modeling and Shrinkage for User Session Length Prediction in Media Streaming
item.description:
Researchers published hierarchical modeling with shrinkage for user session length prediction in media streaming. The approach uses Bayesian hierarchical models to predict how long users will engage with streaming content, enabling better ad inventory forecasting.

Session length prediction is valuable for ad systems because it determines how many ad impressions are available during a user session. Accurate predictions enable better ad pacing and inventory management.

The hierarchical shrinkage approach borrows strength across users with similar characteristics, improving predictions for users with limited history. This is particularly valuable for new or infrequent users where individual-level predictions are unreliable.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that session length prediction — often overlooked in favor of CTR/CVR prediction — is valuable for ad inventory management and pacing optimization.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.01440

item.title: Auto-bidding in Real-Time Auctions via Oracle Imitation Learning (OIL)
item.description:
Researchers published OIL (Oracle Imitation Learning) for auto-bidding in real-time auctions. The approach learns bidding policies by imitating an oracle that has access to perfect information about auction outcomes.

Traditional auto-bidding approaches use RL or optimization-based methods, but these can be unstable or require extensive online experimentation. OIL learns from logged auction data by imitating what the optimal bid would have been, providing a more stable training signal.

For practitioners, OIL offers a practical alternative to online RL for auto-bidding. By learning from historical data with oracle supervision, the approach avoids the risks and costs of online experimentation while still learning effective bidding strategies.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.11434

item.title: Expert-Guided Diffusion Planner for Auto-Bidding in Online Advertising
item.description:
Researchers published an expert-guided diffusion planner for auto-bidding that uses diffusion models to generate bidding trajectories. The approach leverages expert demonstrations to guide the diffusion process, generating high-quality bidding strategies.

Diffusion models have shown remarkable results in generating high-quality samples across domains. Applying them to auto-bidding allows the system to generate diverse bidding strategies that explore the space of possible approaches, then select the best one for each auction.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that generative models can be applied to sequential decision-making problems like auto-bidding. The expert-guided approach ensures that generated strategies are reasonable while still allowing exploration of novel approaches.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08687

item.title: Lightweight Auto-Bidding Based on Traffic Prediction in Live Advertising
item.description:
Researchers published a lightweight auto-bidding approach based on traffic prediction for live advertising. The system predicts future traffic patterns to optimize bidding strategies, enabling more efficient budget allocation across time periods.

Live advertising (real-time ad auctions) requires bidding decisions within milliseconds. By predicting traffic patterns, the system can make more informed decisions about how much to bid now versus saving budget for later periods with potentially higher-value opportunities.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that traffic prediction can improve auto-bidding performance. Understanding when high-value opportunities are likely to occur enables better budget pacing and bid optimization.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06069

item.title: Enhancing Generative Auto-Bidding with Offline Reward Evaluation and Policy Search
item.description:
Researchers published a method for enhancing generative auto-bidding with offline reward evaluation and policy search. The approach improves generative bidding models by providing better evaluation signals during training, enabling more effective policy optimization.

Generative auto-bidding models learn to generate bidding strategies, but evaluating the quality of generated strategies is challenging without online deployment. Offline reward evaluation provides a proxy for online performance, enabling the model to improve without costly online experimentation.

The policy search component explores the space of possible strategies more effectively, finding better solutions than random sampling or simple optimization approaches.

For practitioners, this work addresses a key challenge in generative auto-bidding: how to evaluate and improve generated strategies offline. The combination of offline reward evaluation and policy search provides a practical framework for training better bidding models without online experimentation costs.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15927
